track.name: Python Basics
track.description: The core building blocks of Python — variables, types, collections, control flow, and functions — that every other Python topic rests on.

cards.title: What is Python?
cards.explanation: Python is a general-purpose programming language built around readability — the syntax stays out of your way so you can focus on the logic. It's the default language for AI, data work, scripting, and a huge chunk of the modern web backend.
cards.takeaway: Python: clean syntax, runs almost everything.

cards.title: Indentation is syntax
cards.explanation: Most languages use braces or keywords to mark code blocks — Python uses indentation, usually 4 spaces. Mixing tabs and spaces or being inconsistent doesn't just look messy, it actually breaks the program.
cards.takeaway: In Python, whitespace is part of the grammar.

cards.title: Variables are labels, not boxes
cards.explanation: A variable in Python is just a name that points to a value — you don't declare a type, you just assign with `=` and Python figures it out. The same name can later point to a totally different value or even a different type.
cards.takeaway: Variables hold references, not fixed types.

cards.title: The core data types
cards.explanation: Python ships with a small set of types you'll use constantly: int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict, set. Most bugs in early code come from confusing one for another — like treating a number as a string after reading user input.
cards.takeaway: Know your types — half of debugging is type confusion.

cards.title: Strings are immutable
cards.explanation: Strings are text wrapped in single, double, or triple quotes. They're immutable, meaning every 'edit' — uppercase, replace, slice — actually returns a brand new string instead of changing the original.
cards.takeaway: String operations return new strings, not edits.

cards.title: Numbers: int vs float
cards.explanation: Python has int (whole numbers) and float (decimals), and it auto-promotes int to float when needed. Dividing two ints with `/` always gives a float; use `//` when you want integer division.
cards.takeaway: `/` gives a float, `//` gives an int.

cards.title: Truthy and falsy values
cards.explanation: True and False are the boolean values, but almost any value can act like one in a condition. Empty strings, 0, None, empty lists, and empty dicts all count as False — everything else is True.
cards.takeaway: Empty or zero things are falsy.

cards.title: Lists: ordered and mutable
cards.explanation: Lists are ordered collections written with [] — you can mix types, change items in place, and grow or shrink them anytime. They're the default 'a bunch of things' container in Python.

cards.title: Tuples: lists that can't change
cards.explanation: Tuples look like lists but use () and are immutable — once created, you can't add, remove, or replace items. Use them for fixed groupings like coordinates, return values, or anything you want to safely hand around.

cards.title: Dictionaries: key → value lookups
cards.explanation: Dicts store key-value pairs in {} and are how you model anything with named fields — a user, a config, an API response. Lookups by key are nearly instant, no matter how big the dict gets.
cards.takeaway: Dicts: named lookups, fast at any size.

cards.title: Sets: unique items only
cards.explanation: Sets are unordered collections that automatically drop duplicates. They're perfect for deduplication and 'is X in here?' checks, which run far faster than scanning a list.
cards.takeaway: Sets: unique items, instant membership checks.

cards.title: if / elif / else
cards.explanation: if, elif, and else let your code branch based on conditions. Python evaluates them top-down and runs the first branch whose condition is true — the rest are skipped, even if they'd also match.
cards.takeaway: First matching branch wins; the rest are skipped.

cards.title: for loops iterate, not count
cards.explanation: Python's for loop walks through any iterable — lists, strings, dicts, ranges — handing you one item at a time. You don't manage an index counter; you just loop over the thing itself.
cards.takeaway: Loop over the thing, not over an index.

cards.title: while loops
cards.explanation: A while loop keeps running as long as its condition stays true. Use it when you don't know how many iterations you'll need — reading until end-of-file, retrying until success, polling until ready.
cards.takeaway: while = loop until the condition fails.

cards.title: Functions with def
cards.explanation: Functions are defined with `def`, take parameters, and optionally return a value with `return`. They're the main tool for avoiding repetition and keeping code testable — if you've written the same logic twice, it probably wants to be a function.
cards.takeaway: Wrote it twice? Make it a function.

cards.title: print() and input()
cards.explanation: `print()` sends output to the terminal; `input()` pauses the program and reads one line from the user. The catch: `input()` always returns a string, so wrap it in `int()` or `float()` when you need a number.
cards.takeaway: input() always gives you a string.

cards.title: Comments: explain the why
cards.explanation: Single-line comments start with `#`; for longer notes people often use triple-quoted strings. Good comments explain *why* code does something — the code itself already shows *what* it does.
cards.takeaway: Comment the why, not the what.
